questions.q: Why is "instrument everything" not a workable strategy, according to this lesson?
options: It trades "not enough data" for "too much data to search," while raising the telemetry bill, often to the point of rivaling the compute bill
Cloud providers technically forbid emitting more than one metric per service
Metrics, logs, and traces cannot technically coexist in the same system
Instrumentation has no cost at all, so the only downside is development time
questions.explain: Indiscriminate instrumentation buries the signal that matters inside volume nobody can search, and it's billed by volume, which can make the observability bill rival the compute bill.

questions.q: According to the lesson's framework, which component deserves the deepest instrumentation — metrics, structured logs, and trace spans together?
options: Whichever component was written most recently
An internal admin tool used only by the team itself
A business-critical path, such as checkout or payment, where failure has direct revenue or trust impact
Whichever component has the simplest code
questions.explain: Instrumentation depth should track business consequence of failure — checkout, auth, and payment flows earn the full treatment; low-impact internal tools don't need the same depth.

questions.q: In the lesson's Redis example, why is instrumenting cache_pool_active_connections and cache_pool_wait_time_ms described as "targeted"?
options: Because it was added automatically by a framework default
Because it's shaped specifically around how that cache already failed before — connection pool exhaustion — rather than guessing at what might go wrong
Because every metric in the system uses that exact naming convention
Because it replaces the need for any logging around the cache entirely
questions.explain: The second framework question is about known failure points: instrumenting around a documented past failure closes a gap you've already seen, rather than speculating broadly.

questions.q: What makes attaching a raw user_id as a metric label risky, compared to putting it in a log field?
options: Metric labels are always encrypted while log fields are not
user_id cannot be parsed as a string in most logging libraries
Metrics are deleted automatically after 24 hours regardless of label values
Every distinct label value creates a new time series, so a high-cardinality label like a raw user ID can silently explode one metric into millions of series
questions.explain: High-cardinality labels are a specific, costly trap — metrics stay cheap because they're low-cardinality; logs and traces are where high-cardinality detail like a user ID belongs.

questions.q: What is "alert fatigue," as described in this lesson?
options: A hardware limitation that prevents more than a fixed number of alerts per day
The erosion of trust in alerts and dashboards caused by too many low-value signals competing with the few that actually matter
A billing term specific to one cloud provider's monitoring product
The automatic muting of all alerts after business hours
questions.explain: A dashboard with 200 flat panels buries the 15 that actually move when something's wrong — that dilution of attention, not a technical limit, is what alert fatigue describes.
